Your work recalls the Eliza effect and dangers of anthropomorphization. Yet, Claude is a different magnitude of complexity and intelligence compared to Eliza. Does that distinction matter? Do you have a theory of consciousness? Can that include machines?

Do you have a theory of consciousness that could include machines?

The internet became your reality. You said to Art Basel , "As artists, we cannot compete with the Internet’s super-fast, ever-changing flow of images, ideas, and stimuli. There’s no point in trying to re-create that speed, that energy. What we can do is select one thing and isolate it from the rest to produce a moment of reflection on these processes – even if only for a minute." How have you adapted this strategy with AI?

How does isolating one thing for reflection work in the age of AI?

You’ve engaged artistically with net.art and the rise of the internet, the introduction of social media and post-internet. Now with AI and the automatization of intelligence you see the full automation of the self. Where are we headed with the pace of the automation of the self we’re experiencing? What’s left to automate? Is there any hope across that transformation you’ve witnessed from net.art to neural net slop?

Where is the automation of the self headed, and what’s left to automate?

The argument about copying and the degradation of the original goes back at least to Plato versus Aristotle. It resurfaces with Duchamp, Benjamin, Berger, and the pervasive copy culture of early internet. You copied others and made your own work freely copyable, inspired by the open-source movement. But as you noted, again to Art Basel , that "naive dream of complete accessibility slowly turned into a nightmare of self-design — to correct, adapt, and contradict that image." Copying again is at the center of the AI ethics debate. How do you think about copying in the age of AI?
